Global summary

On 2026-07-08 the physical host running azlsapgvpdb02 (node 01ea29c8-4e86-cb82-9ce0-6ed35c673d5b) developed a hardware fault (memory errors / crashes) and was marked Degraded → Unallocatable at 20:35. The Azure platform reacted by live-migrating the VM to a healthy node (df6c4d5b-0ce9-2abf-17ee-78022e30d2ed): placement at 20:50:23, an Infrastructure-initiated LiveMigration scheduled event (Freeze all) from 20:51:23, a cutover freeze of ~1.8 s at 21:10, and completion at 21:16:16 (root cause “UnallocatableNode / bad hardware health”). This is a production P&G SAP Oracle DB (SOX-regulated, Highly Restricted), so even a sub-2 second freeze can be felt.

RCA candidate 1 — internal

Most likely explanation. There was no reboot (Reboot Detail = No data; no red dots on the Scheduled Events & Reboots graph) and no outage in region East US. The one impactful event was a platform-initiated live migration: the host node the VM was running on (01ea29c8-4e86-cb82-9ce0-6ed35c673d5b) failed a hardware health check (memory faults / crashes) and was declared Degraded → Unallocatable at 20:35 on 2026-07-08. The VM was reactively migrated to a healthy node (df6c4d5b-0ce9-2abf-17ee-78022e30d2ed): placement 20:50:23, Infrastructure LiveMigration scheduled event 20:51:23–21:17:03 (Freeze all), a measured guest freeze of ~1.8 s at 21:10, and completion 21:16:16. TriggerType UnallocatableNode, RCA “Bad hardware health”; IsCustomerInitiatedOperation=false, isGuestOsCrash=false.

Customer context. azlsapgvpdb02 is a large-memory Standard_M32bds_v3 running an Oracle database on Linux, tagged Azure SAP Prod / Stage=Prod, SOX-regulated, Highly Restricted, supporting the Supply Chain (NA) application and administered by SAP CTE DBA teams. Clustered/HA database workloads of this kind are highly sensitive to even sub-second pauses: a ~1.8 s live-migration blackout can be enough for a cluster manager (e.g. Pacemaker) or the database's own HA layer to interpret the freeze as a node failure and fence/fail over the node — which surfaces to the customer as an unexpected stop, and can even appear later as a “customer initiated” restart if a fencing agent acted.

Ruled-out factors. Performance was not implicated: CPU ~1–8%, memory pressure ≤10%, ~125 GB RAM free, disk BW/IOPS consumption in the low single digits; disk queue/latency showed only isolated transient spikes unrelated to the migration time.

Suggested further investigation. (1) Confirm the exact time the customer observed the disruption and correlate against the ~21:10 UTC cutover. (2) Pull guest OS and Oracle/cluster logs around 2026-07-08 21:05–21:20 UTC for fencing, failover, evictions or I/O-freeze messages. (3) Verify whether an HA/cluster fencing action occurred and, if so, tune cluster/corosync timeouts to tolerate short live-migration blackouts. (4) Check for any dependency on external services that could have compounded the pause.

RCA candidate 2 — customer-facing (draft)

Summary. On 8 July 2026, at approximately 21:10 UTC, your virtual machine was briefly paused while the Azure platform relocated it to alternative physical hardware as an automated protective maintenance action. The virtual machine was not restarted by the platform and remained available before and after the operation.

Root Cause. The physical host on which the virtual machine was running began to show early indicators of a hardware issue. To protect the workload, Azure automatically live-migrated the virtual machine to healthy hardware. Live migration involves a very short pause (in this case approximately two seconds) while memory and state are transferred. No platform outage was detected in the region during this period, and no platform-initiated operating-system reboot occurred.

Resolution. The virtual machine was successfully relocated to healthy hardware and the affected host was taken out of service. No customer action is required, and the virtual machine continues to run normally.

Customer Impact. A single, brief pause of approximately two seconds around 21:10 UTC on 8 July 2026. For most workloads this is transparent; however, highly sensitive clustered or high-availability configurations may react to such a brief pause — for example by initiating a failover — which could be perceived as an unexpected stop. We recommend reviewing application and cluster logs around this time to confirm whether any such failover was triggered.
